podcast.title: Challenging Band Dynamics
podcast.body: The band comprised Mike McCready (recovering alcoholic and drug addict), John Baker Saunders (who also had addiction issues), Layne Staley (Alice in Chains frontman, notorious drug addict), and Barrett Martin (Screaming Trees drummer, noted for his stability and academic background). Despite the varied personal struggles, the band managed to function. "Singing for the band was lain stately of Alice and Chains, a guy who had a reputation as being the biggest drug addict in a city of drug addicts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation in Rehab
podcast.body: Mad Season was formed after Mike McCready (Pearl Jam) met bassist John Baker Saunders during rehab at the Hazelden Rehabilitation Center in Minneapolis. They bonded over their shared struggles and decided to form a band in Seattle upon their release. "They bonded in rehab and decided that when they got out, they would form a band, back home in Seattle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Loss of Members
podcast.body: The band experienced tragic losses, with John Baker Saunders dying of a heroin overdose on January 15, 1999, and Layne Staley later dying from drug-related causes. "John Baker Saunders died of a hair run overdose on January 15, 1999."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Academic and Artistic Pursuits
xref.body: Barrett Martin, the drummer for Screaming Trees and Mad Season, is described as highly intelligent, holding bachelor's and master's degrees in anthropology, linguistics, and ethnomusicology, and was an honor student. He also became a Zen artist. "Bachelors and master's degrees in anthropology, linguistics, and ethnomusicology, and an honor student."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Participation in Mad Season Project
xref.body: Despite his severe addiction, Layne Staley managed to participate in the Mad Season project. Mike McCready and John Baker Saunders supported him through the recording sessions, hoping that working with sober musicians might offer him a moment of clarity, but it ultimately did not help him achieve lasting sobriety. "Mike McCready and John Baker Saunders pulled Lane through those sessions, hoping that being around sober musicians would produce a moment of clarity, but it didn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
